Archibald Brown
ahr'chi-bald broun
n. (Archibald Geikie Brown, 1844–1922, Spurgeon's student, pastor of the East London Tabernacle, and author of The Devil's Mission of Amusement)
Germanic Erkanbald, genuinely bold; English Brown, of brown complexion.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Archibald Brown was converted in his teens, trained at Spurgeon's Pastors' College, and in 1866 became pastor of a small Baptist church in Stepney that grew under his ministry into the East London Tabernacle, a congregation of some three thousand in one of the poorest districts of London. His work among the East End poor, through mission halls, relief for the destitute in the hard winters, and ministry to dock labourers and their families, was as remarkable as his preaching. He stood with Spurgeon throughout the Downgrade Controversy and was among his closest friends. He is best remembered for a pamphlet, The Devil's Mission of Amusement, in which he argued that providing entertainment to draw people to church was nowhere commanded by Christ, nowhere practised by the apostles, and wholly unable to do what the gospel does; the early church, he observed, turned the world upside down without it. From 1907 to 1911 Brown was pastor of the Metropolitan Tabernacle itself. His argument was the apostles': the Thessalonians “turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God” (1Th 1:9) under preaching, and the apostolic church “continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine” (Act 2:42).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines amusement as that which amuses, detains or engages the mind, entertainment.

expand to see more

AMUSE'MENT, n. That which amuses, detains or engages the mind; entertainment of the mind; pastime.

TAB'ERNACLE, n. A tent; a place of worship; a sacred place.

DES'TITUTE, a. Not having or possessing; wanting; in need of the necessaries of life.

Key Scripture

1Th 1:9 — "For they themselves shew of us what manner of entering in we had unto you, and how ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God;"

Act 2:42 — "And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers."

1Co 2:4 — "And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power:"

Mat 11:28 — "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."

Modern Corruption

An East End pastor who called church entertainment the devil's mission.

expand to see more

The dictionary names the corruption Brown attacked as the attempt to win the world to the church by entertainment, which has since become the method of much of evangelicalism. Brown's point was exegetical: Christ sent His disciples to preach, not to amuse, and His invitation is to rest in Him, “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Mat 11:28), not to diversion. A church that must entertain people to keep them has already conceded that the gospel is not enough.

His own ministry answers the objection that plain preaching cannot reach the poor. He preached the gospel in the poorest district in London to thousands, and fed the hungry beside it. The principle to recover is Paul's: power in preaching is “not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power” (1Co 2:4).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek epistrepho (G1994), to turn; proskartereo (G4342), to continue stedfastly; anapauo (G373), to give rest.

Greek eidolon (G1497) — an idol; 1 Thessalonians 1:9.

Greek proskartereo (G4342) — to continue stedfastly; Acts 2:42.

Usage

"“turned to God from idols” (1Th 1:9) — conversion without amusement."

"“continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine” (Act 2:42) — what held the first church."

"“I will give you rest” (Mat 11:28) — the gospel's offer, not the world's."
